summary: Help Year 4 children (age 8–9) move from naming quadrilaterals by appearance to deciding category membership by property tests, and begin class-inclusion reasoning: a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it passes every rectangle test (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus has the extra property of four equal sides. The core obstacle is partition/prototype thinking — a child files each shape in exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't match the 'long oblong' they picture. Teaching shifts the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?'
misconceptions: A square is not a rectangle — they are two different, separate kinds of shape (exclusive/partition thinking)
A rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square cannot be one (oblong prototype; the unequal-sides attribute is wrongly treated as defining)
A shape can only belong to one category, so it cannot be a rectangle AND a square at the same time
A square turned 45° is a 'diamond', not a square (orientation bound to the prototype)

activities.title: Sort and stretch: does the shape pass the rectangle tests?
steps: Take a plain quadrilateral and adjust its corners until all four angles are right angles (check with a set-square); confirm whether opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Run the rectangle checklist item by item — '4 right angles? ✓ opposite sides equal and parallel? ✓' — and place the shape inside the 'rectangle' ring of a nested diagram when it passes all tests.

Now, starting from a rectangle with all four sides equal (a square), pull one pair of opposite sides longer while keeping all four right angles, so the shape stays a rectangle but is no longer a square; then shorten them, still keeping the right angles, until all four sides are equal again and watch it move into the innermost 'square' region nested inside 'rectangle', which is nested inside 'quadrilateral'.
Say out loud, in your own words, why the SAME shape can sit in two boxes at once ('it is a rectangle because... and also a square because...').
Repeat with a rhombus checklist to see the square also sits inside 'rhombus' where the rings overlap.
activities.insight: Category membership is decided by which property tests a shape passes, not by how it looks; a square passes every rectangle test, so a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) — and one shape can belong to two nested categories at once.

activities.title: Predict, test, explain with a real square
steps: Before testing, predict whether a square 'counts as' a rectangle and say WHY.
Check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler: four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel?
If the result differs from your prediction, explain what changed your mind.

Answer probing questions: Does it matter how long the sides are? Is a square turned to look like a diamond still a square and still a rectangle? Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?
Decide whether a square is also a special rhombus, and justify.
activities.insight: Stating a reason before testing exposes prototype thinking; reconciling a 'no, too square' prediction with the square passing every rectangle test is where the concept takes hold. The asymmetry — you can draw a rectangle that is not a square, but not a square that is not a rectangle — is the tell of genuine understanding.

activities.title: Draw the exceptions and defend the claim
steps: Draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, and say which defining property it is missing for EACH of those three categories.
Draw a rectangle that is not a square.
Explain to a sceptical 'shape detective' why a square still counts as a rectangle even though it doesn't look like a long oblong, citing the defining properties it passes.
Sort a mixed set of quadrilaterals (including a square, a 45°-tilted rectangle, and a nearly-square rectangle) into a nested/overlapping Venn, justifying each placement by properties.
activities.insight: Reasoning about which properties are ABSENT (for non-examples) and which are PRESENT (for inclusion) consolidates definition-based classification and loosens the oblong prototype.

checkQuestion: Show the child a square (and, alongside, an oblong rectangle). Ask: 'Is this square also a rectangle?' — then, whatever they answer: 'How do you know? What makes something a rectangle?'
checkAnswer: Yes — a square is a rectangle. A rectangle needs four right angles and opposite sides that are equal and parallel; a square has all of those, plus its four sides happen to be equal too, so it is a special kind of rectangle.
